name: monostate
intent: Make every instance of a class share one body of state, so clients construct, pass and destroy ordinary objects while the data behaves as a single application-wide value - singularity of state without the static accessor or the single-instance constraint.
problem: A class's data must be application-wide (a shared configuration, registry, pool or facility), but callers should not have to route through a static accessor or a single published object: containers, serializers and UI frameworks instantiate the class themselves, and call sites should read like ordinary object code. Making the fields static hides the sharing behind a normal instance interface - and drags in the test-seam, thread-safety and one-way-conversion problems that come with shared mutable state.
context: Object-oriented code where the singularity is intrinsic to the concept (a process-wide facility) rather than to a use site, where a container or framework must be able to call a public constructor, and where subclasses are expected to vary behaviour over one shared set of variables (Martin's turnstile). It is a same-process mechanism: the state is per process, JVM, application domain or runtime realm, never distributed.
benefits: Transparency: clients use an ordinary public constructor and ordinary instance methods - no Instance() accessor, no lifetime protocol, and no call site that has to acknowledge it is touching application-wide state.

Identity-indifferent state: any number of short-lived instances can be created and destroyed without duplicating or losing the data; the state's lifetime is the program's while the instances' lifetime is the call site's.

Polymorphism and derivability: the methods stay non-static, so subclasses can override behaviour while every derivative still shares the same variables - something a class of static utility methods cannot do.

Well-defined creation and destruction of the state: static (or class-level, lazily initialized) storage has a deterministic lifetime, so there is no null instance to check and no lazy-Singleton double-initialization race.

Cheap migration path: a class becomes a monostate by moving its data to static storage and keeps its whole public interface, and it is the only shared-state form available to code that a container instantiates itself without the client opting in.
tradeoffs: It is global state with better manners: the sharing is invisible in the type, the constructor and the call site, so any code holding an instance can mutate what every other part of the program sees.
Every write is a concurrent write: shared mutable storage needs explicit synchronization, and reads and writes from different threads race even though each instance is truthfully 'local'.

Tests share the state: there is no per-test instance that can be constructed fresh, so suites become order-dependent unless a reset seam is added, and the state cannot be replaced with a fake the way an injected dependency can.

One-way conversion: a non-monostate class cannot be turned into one by derivation, and once the solution depends on the shared variables (Martin's turnstile) supporting more than one state later means restructuring - the fix is a redesign, not a subclass.

Process-local and present: the state cannot span JVMs, application domains, realms or machines, so it is not a distribution mechanism, and its storage is allocated for the whole run even if the class is never used.

participants.responsibility: Declares the ordinary instance interface and holds all data in static (class-level) storage; nothing in its public shape reveals that instances share state.
An ordinary object created through the public constructor; it carries identity but no per-instance data, and its methods read and write the class's shared storage.
The single copy of the data living at class/module scope with the lifetime of the program (or lazy initialization); created and destroyed independently of any instance.
A subclass that overrides behaviour (or declares per-class storage where the language allows it) while remaining part of the same monostate over the shared variables.

use_cases: Process-wide facilities that are configured once and then read everywhere - log level and sink, metrics registry, default timeout or retry policy - while callers still use ordinary objects.
Shared resource pools and load balancers where the pool contents and a round-robin cursor are process-wide but the class is used as an ordinary collaborator (the canonical LoadBalancer example).
Framework- or container-managed types: JavaBeans, serializers and DI containers instantiate the class themselves, so a static accessor is not available even though the state must be application-wide.
State machines whose many short-lived facades share one set of variables and whose states are modelled as subclasses overriding behaviour over that shared data (Martin's turnstile).

Incremental refactoring of a legacy global into an object-shaped API: keep the static storage, wrap it in a class with an ordinary constructor, and replace the storage with an injected dependency later without touching call sites.
EnTT's entt::monostate<id_type> provides keyed, type-differentiated static storage for process-wide configuration; use it when many lightweight handles must observe one typed setting.
Boost.Test documents boost/test/framework.hpp as a Mono-state Unit Test Framework interface, centralizing test-unit registration, execution and observers behind ordinary framework calls.
The Python monostate package supplies a Borg-style shared-state base across instances and subclasses, useful when plugin or container code creates many facades over one process-local setting.
avoid_when: The state has one owner and one lifecycle: create one instance in main and pass it (Just Create One / dependency injection) - simpler than either Singleton or Monostate.
Tests, requests or tenants need independent state: construct the data per test/request/tenant and inject it; the shared form cannot be isolated without a bespoke reset.
The data is immutable configuration: use constants or a readonly value handed in, not shared mutable static storage.

A single instance is genuinely the constraint and an accessor is acceptable: Singleton states the structural constraint where readers can see it, while Monostate hides the sharing - choose the one your readers can see.
The state must be coordinated across processes or machines: use durable storage or an explicit distributed-state mechanism instead of a per-process monostate.
anti_patterns: Stealth singleton: using a normal-looking class to hide an application-wide mutable dependency, so the coupling is invisible in every signature and review.
Per-instance configuration that is silently global: a constructor or setter parameter that writes shared static state, so the second new Config(x) overwrites the first call's settings.
Request-, user- or tenant-scoped data ('the current user') kept in shared state, so concurrent requests overwrite each other's context.
Tests that rely on leftover static state as an implicit fixture, turning the suite into an order-dependent sequence.
Public mutable static fields exposed as the API, so any code can reassign the shared storage instead of going through behaviour.
design_principles: Explicit sharing: transparency is a documentation obligation - if state is shared, the type that owns it must say so, and reviewers must treat it as global state.
Separate identity from state: identity belongs to instances, state to the concept; decide deliberately which of the two the design actually needs.
Encapsulation: keep the shared storage private and expose behaviour, never a public mutable class member.
Prefer explicit dependencies (dependency inversion, least knowledge) whenever the shared state could be handed in; Monostate earns its place only when the singularity is intrinsic to the concept.
Keep substitution possible: a hidden global makes an object behave differently under test than in production, so preserve a seam (holder, interface, reset).
best_practices: Document on the type (and in review) that all instances share one body of state; nothing else in the code signals it.
Keep the shared state private, enforce its invariants in the accessors, and guard every mutation with the language's concurrency primitives - locks, atomics, Mutex, synchronized.
Provide a reset or snapshot seam so tests do not inherit each other's writes, and reset in teardown.
Hide the storage behind a small holder or interface so the monostate can be converted to an injected instance later without touching call sites.

Prefer Monostate over Singleton only for what distinguishes it - transparency for container-instantiated classes and polymorphic derivatives over shared state - and otherwise pass one ordinary object around.
sources: Robert C. Martin, Singleton and Monostate (2002) - chapter derived from Agile Software Development: Principles, Patterns, and Practices; all variables static, methods non-static; benefits (transparency, derivability, polymorphism, well-defined lifetime) and counter-consequences (no conversion, presence, platform locality).
Boost.Test's framework.hpp documents a Mono-state Unit Test Framework interface for shared test lifecycle and registration state.
EnTT's entt::monostate implementation uses static per-key, per-type storage for configuration.
Python monostate package implementing Borg-style shared state across instances and subclasses.
Criticism: Google's Testing Blog explains why hidden global state makes singleton-style designs hard to test; the same concern applies to monostate.
Python's contextvars documentation describes context-local isolation for async tasks and threads, the safer alternative when state is scoped to execution context.
Reference guidance distinguishes C++ std::monostate as a zero-state variant utility from the shared-state Monostate idiom.
